n: Near death, Jacob gathers his twelve sons for his final blessings—part blessing, part prophecy about their future tribes, reaching even to “the last days.”

f.g: in days to come; in latter times

n: Jacob calls them to listen. The parallel lines (“sons of Jacob” / “Israel your father”) mark the beginning of a long poem.
Reuben, the firstborn, should have held the place of honor and strength by birthright.
But Reuben was “unstable as water”—uncontrolled—and lost his birthright for sleeping with his father’s concubine Bilhah. The birthright went to Joseph.

f.w: thou wentest up to thy father's bed

n: Simeon and Levi are paired as brothers in violence. Their swords were weapons of cruelty, recalling their massacre at Shechem.
Jacob distances himself from their violent plans. In anger they killed men and maimed oxen (“digged down a wall” is better read “hamstrung an ox”).

Jacob curses their anger, not the men themselves. They would be scattered: Simeon was absorbed into Judah, and Levi received no land—yet Levi’s scattering became a blessing as the priestly tribe living among all Israel.

f.w: I will divide them in Jacob

n: Judah’s name sounds like “praise,” and his brothers will praise him. He will triumph over enemies and his brothers will bow to him—fulfilled in the kings of David’s line.

f.g: wordplay on Yehudah (Judah) and yodukha (they shall praise you)

n: Judah is pictured as a lion—young and strong, then crouching at rest after the hunt, too fearsome to disturb. Jesus is called “the Lion of the tribe of Juda.”

A key messianic prophecy: royal rule would remain with Judah until “Shiloh” comes, to whom the nations will gather. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, see this fulfilled in Jesus Christ, born of Judah.

f.g: a ruler’s staff, symbol of kingship
Meaning debated: perhaps “he to whom it belongs,” or “the peaceful one.”

n: Judah’s land will be so rich in vineyards that one could tie a donkey to a choice vine and wash clothes in wine. The image of garments red with “the blood of grapes” is echoed in prophecies of Christ’s Second Coming.
Eyes dark with wine and teeth white with milk—a picture of overflowing abundance.

f.g: Hebrew may mean “darker than wine” or “dull from wine.”

n: Zebulun would live near the sea and benefit from shipping and trade, with territory reaching toward the Phoenician coast.
Issachar is compared to a strong donkey resting between saddlebags—hardworking but content.

f.g: lying down between the saddlebags (or sheepfolds)

n: Issachar would love the comfort of good land so much that it would accept forced labor to keep it.
Dan’s name means “judge.” Though descended from a handmaid, Dan would govern itself as a true tribe of Israel. Samson came from Dan.
Dan is pictured as a small snake striking a horse’s heel—small but dangerous, able to bring down a larger foe.
In the middle of the blessings Jacob breaks into a short prayer, expressing his hope in the Lord’s deliverance. It is the first time the word “salvation” (yeshuah) appears in the Bible.

f.g: Hebrew yeshuah — closely related to the name Jesus (Yeshua)

n: Gad’s name sounds like the Hebrew for “raid.” Raiders would attack Gad, but Gad would strike back and win.

f.g: wordplay: gad, gedud (raiders), yegudennu (shall raid him)

n: Asher (“happy”) would enjoy rich food and produce delicacies fit for a king.
Naphtali is like a free-running deer, swift and graceful, and will speak beautiful words.

f.g: beautiful words (or, in some readings, “lovely fawns”)

n: Joseph is a fruitful branch by a spring whose branches run over the wall. Latter-day Saints see this fulfilled in part as Lehi’s family, descendants of Joseph, crossed the sea to the Americas.

f.g: a fruitful branch; wordplay on Ephraim (“fruitful”)

f.w: whose branches run over the wall

n: Joseph was attacked by “archers”—a picture of his brothers’ hatred, Potiphar’s wife’s lies, and his unjust imprisonment.
Yet Joseph stood firm, strengthened by “the Mighty One of Jacob.” Jacob calls God the Shepherd and the Stone (Rock) of Israel—titles later applied to Christ.

f.g: Hebrew ’abir Ya‘aqob, “the Mighty One of Jacob”

f.w: the shepherd, the stone of Israel

n: Joseph will receive blessings from heaven above (rain), the deep below (springs), and the breasts and womb (many children)—fullness of every kind of blessing.

f.w: blessings of the deep that lieth under

n: Jacob’s blessings on Joseph surpass even those his fathers received, reaching to “the everlasting hills.” Joseph, once separated from his brothers, now receives the crown blessing.

f.w: the utmost bound of the everlasting hills
him that was separate from his brethren
f.g: Hebrew nazir — set apart, consecrated; perhaps “prince among his brothers.”

n: Benjamin is a fierce wolf, devouring prey morning and night. The tribe was known for warriors, including King Saul and, later, the apostle Paul.
These twelve blessings define the twelve tribes of Israel. Each received a blessing suited to him—the pattern behind patriarchal blessings in the Church today.

f.w: every one according to his blessing

n: Jacob charges his sons to bury him with his fathers in Canaan. “Gathered unto my people” expresses belief in joining loved ones after death.

f.w: I am to be gathered unto my people
f.g: an idiom for death and reunion with ancestors

n: He describes the exact location: the cave of Machpelah near Mamre (Hebron), the only land Abraham legally owned in Canaan.
Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah were buried there. Leah, not Rachel, rests with Jacob—quiet honor for the unloved wife and mother of Judah and Levi.
Jacob stresses that the land was legally purchased from the Hittites—a small foothold of the promised land.
When he finished, Jacob drew his feet onto the bed, breathed his last, and was gathered to his people—a peaceful death after a long, hard life.
